milestone.title: Subsystem Extraction — Bounded Repository Program
milestone.description: End-to-end decomposition of Runalith into bounded GitHub repositories while retaining nplongx/runalith as the composition host. Includes contract stabilization, Workflow ownership/API gates, Trust & Evidence, Execution, Workspace, Adaptive Goal, Agent, API adapter and Dashboard extraction, plus host integration and compatibility acceptance. Repository extraction does not imply separate processes or databases. No production data migration, trust-state mutation, process restart, package publication or release authorization is included without a separate explicit owner decision.

items.body:
## Objective
Publish a stable Workflow-owned command/query boundary that downstream subsystems can consume without importing private Workflow implementation modules.

## Scope
- Define Workflow lifecycle APIs for proposal, approval, immutable plan, task, artifact, event and policy/role reads/writes.
- Separate pure DTO/schema contracts from stateful registry, compiler and lifecycle behavior.
- Replace remaining AGG imports of deep Workflow plan/role implementation paths with Workflow Contracts and narrow versioned Workflow query/command APIs.
- Replace the transitional caller-managed `beginExecutionSpawnAuthorization` / `commitExecutionSpawnAuthorization` / `rollbackExecutionSpawnAuthorization` sequence with one Workflow-owned atomic command.
- Document stable error codes, idempotency identity, retryability, cancellation, timeout and unknown-outcome semantics.

## Acceptance criteria
- Public API has a versioned root entrypoint and no raw `DatabaseSync`, SQL, mutable DB handle or internal authorization marker.
- Every cross-boundary operation has a named owner, request/response DTO, stable error contract and explicit consistency semantics.
- AGG planning no longer imports private Workflow plan/role modules; import-boundary tests reject regressions.
- Spawn authorization is one atomic Workflow command with exact plan/approval/task binding and regression tests for stale approval, duplicate request and uncertain outcome.
- Real consumers compile and pass contract tests using only the public API; no test-only adapter substitutes for production consumers.

## Guardrails
Workflow remains the only authority for approval and immutable execution plans. This issue does not change approval policy, dispatch authority, production state or physical database identity.

items.title: CI: test only affected Rust packages and their reverse dependencies
items.body:
Rust always runs `cargo test --workspace`. The workspace graph allows narrower selection: `khipu-lsp` has no consumer, a PostgreSQL driver change does not affect the MySQL driver, `khipu-engine` and `khipu-driver-core` do affect everything.

**Proposal**
- Planner computes changed workspace packages from `cargo metadata --no-deps` and their reverse-dependency closure (normal, build, dev and platform deps).
- Explicit extra relationships the Cargo graph cannot see: support JSON embedded in Rust, corpus files read at runtime, `backend.test.ts` / `lib.rs` cross-language source inspection, the `generated` suite launching Vitest.
- Root manifests, lockfile, toolchain and uncertain feature changes select the whole workspace. Keep `--locked` and clippy `--all-targets`.
- Rust package selection stays separate from SQL engine selection (server-tests depends on both drivers).
- Full workspace nightly and on release.

**Acceptance criteria**
- Planner fixtures for PostgreSQL, MySQL, driver-core, engine, terminal (desktop) and LSP changes, including renamed and deleted packages.

items.title: generate_repo_overview: show dependency freshness and reverse dependencies on detail pages
items.body:
## Why

Repository detail pages should make it easy to answer two questions: “Are this repository's dependencies up to date?” and “Which repositories consume this repository, and at which version?” This helps maintainers plan dependency updates and understand the impact of a new release or change.

For example, https://eclipse-score.github.io/.github/baselibs/index.html currently lists dependencies under “Dependencies: HEAD vs. Release”. That compares the dependency declarations in baselibs' own default branch and latest release; it does not show whether newer versions of those dependencies are available or provide a reverse dependency view.

## Expected behavior

### Dependencies used by this repository

Extend the detail page with dependency information showing:

- Dependency/module name and a link to its source repository and detail page where available.
- The version or commit actually used, including effective Git overrides where applicable.
- The dependency's latest available release and whether it is newer than the version used.
- Whether the dependency's default branch contains newer commits than the consumed revision, ideally including a commits-behind count and a comparison link where the revisions can be resolved.
- Separate release freshness from default-branch freshness: using the latest release can still mean there are newer commits on the default branch.
- Explicit unknown/unavailable states when a source repository or revision cannot be resolved. Diverged history and non-comparable versions must not be presented as “up to date”.

### Repositories using this repository

Add a “Used by” section listing consumers found within the collected repository set:

- Consumer repository, linked to its detail page.
- The version or commit of this repository used by that consumer.
- The consumer ref/context the dependency was read from, clearly distinguishing its default branch and latest release where both are available.

The list should make its collection scope clear; it cannot imply that repositories outside the collected set have been searched.

## Implementation considerations

- Build forward and reverse dependency relationships from the collected dependency declarations and module-to-repository mappings, rather than limiting the view to the small configured list of tracked dependencies.
- Resolve release versions and commit pins against the dependency's own repository and default branch. Preserve the distinction between module/registry versions and GitHub release tags.
- Collect the required metadata into the snapshot so the generated static detail pages work without live API calls.
- Keep repository identities unambiguous across organizations (see #123).

## Acceptance criteria

- A dependency pinned to an older release shows the used version and the newer available release.
- A dependency using its latest release can independently show newer commits on its default branch.
- A Git-pinned dependency is compared using its effective commit rather than an overridden version declaration.
- If repository A uses repository B, B's detail page lists A and the exact version or commit A consumes.
- Multiple consumers using different versions remain distinguishable, and unresolved comparisons are clearly marked.

Related: #85 mentions collecting dependency relationships and a list of repository users; this issue specifies the detail-page behavior and freshness information.

items.title: Reverse dependencies for skills: list dependents, and warn when a version change breaks their range
items.body:
## Problem

Skills can now declare other skills in `dependencies.skills`, and agents already do. But nothing lets you ask the reverse question: **which agents and skills depend on this skill, and on which range?** The only reverse route is `GET /api/integrations/{packageId}/consuming-agents`, and it covers integrations only.

We tested the guards that exist today (cloud, 2026-09-29). We published two throwaway skills, `base@1.0.0` and `consumer@1.0.0`, where `consumer` declares `{"@scope/base": "^1.0.0"}`:

| Action on `base` | Result |
|---|---|
| `DELETE /api/packages/skills/@scope/base` | **409 `in_use`**: "Skill '@scope/base' is used by 1 package(s)". Good, but it doesn't say which package. |
| `DELETE /api/packages/skills/@scope/base/versions/1.0.0` (the only version satisfying `^1.0.0`) | **204, silent.** `base` is left with zero published versions, so `consumer`'s pin is now unsatisfiable. Its next run fails with 422 `dependency_unresolved`. |
| Publish `base@2.0.0` (outside every dependent's range) | **201, silent.** |

The failure mode is real: a scheduled agent that loses a skill breaks at its next run, often unattended.

## Proposal

1. **A dependents route for every package type**, for example `GET /api/packages/{type}/{scope}/{name}/dependents`. It returns the agents and packages declaring it, with the declared range and whether the latest published version still satisfies that range. Expose it in the CLI (`appstrate packages dependents @scope/name`) and in the MCP.
2. **Name the dependents in the existing 409 `in_use`**, so the caller knows what to fix.
3. **Warn, don't block, on version-level changes.** When deleting a version or publishing a new one leaves a dependent's range with no published version to resolve to, the call still succeeds, but the response carries a `warnings` entry listing the affected dependents and ranges. The UI shows it before confirming. Refusing would be too strict: a breaking major or a yanked version is often exactly what the author means to do.

## Out of scope

Dependencies that are not declared. A skill whose script reads a sibling skill's folder without declaring it stays invisible. We are addressing that on the authoring side: `appstrate/skills`, `appstrate-skill-authoring`, "declare every skill you load or read".

items.title: B3.2 impact: identify exact changed tests targets consumers and bounded reverse dependencies
items.body:
## Parent

#927. Depends on #973. Roadmap: #945 B3.2.

## Objective

Move the material map from package-shaped impact to changed-seam evidence.

## Scope

Detect changed integration tests, `#[cfg(test)]`/`#[test]` regions and names, owning lib/bin/test targets, direct production consumers where mechanically derivable, and bounded reverse dependencies. Preserve direct versus inferred/bounded relations and evidence gaps. Add stable identities usable by proof routing.

## Acceptance

A changed Rust unit test is represented as an exact test seam; owning target and package are correct; consumers/reverse dependencies are separately typed; broad declared test targets do not replace exact seams; ordering is stable; ambiguous symbol/test resolution is explicit; no model-created structural edge enters the map.

## Proof

Unit/integration/test-only/source+test/multi-target/reverse-dependency goldens, ambiguity negatives, PR #921-shaped focused seam, verifier/full validation.

## Non-goals

No repository-contract mirror edges, historical associations, proof ranking, or live scheduler.

## Rollback

Retain B3.1 package map and disable exact-seam enrichment.

items.body:
I know that R Universe will re-attempt to build packages that have failures and that it will rebuild packages that haven't built in a month, but it's less clear to me what happens with reverse dependencies. I'm sorry if I've asked before but this is important for the release, which has been decided for the last week in November. 

For example, if package A imports package B, and I push changes to package B, which passes all checks in R Universe, when does package A get rebuilt if it had passed all checks in its last build? What about packages that might have multiple reverse dependencies.

items.title: Etiquette for dealing with (reverse) dependencies
items.body:
# Topic

Changes in the dependencies of a package can break downstream packages.
How can maintainers of dependencies and reverse dependencies best collaborate?

### Who is the audience?

Maintainer of packages at both ends of the dependency axis: maintainers whose package has many reverse dependencies, maintainers that want to be efficient in their dealing with dependencies.


### Why is this important?

Many aspects of this topic can impede smooth releases and stability of packages

- Learning a dependency might break your package at the last minute;
- Having to inform downstream packages that their usage of a given feature is off label.


### What should be covered?

- How to play on the same team as the dependency cf https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2022/09/playing-on-the-same-team-as-your-dependecy/
- How to keep in touch with developments in the upstream dependencies 
- How to inform maintainers of reverse dependencies

The comm call could discuss the topic at both the small scale (your package has 3 reverse dependencies) and big scale (ggplot2, igraph for instance).


### Suggested speakers or contributors

@krlmlr

### Resources you would recommend to the audience

- https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2022/09/playing-on-the-same-team-as-your-dependecy/
- https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/
- https://devguide.ropensci.org/maintenance_evolution.html
